metadata.title: International pension comparison
metadata.description: A source-linked comparison of pension financing, adequacy, coverage and ageing pressure in Italy, Switzerland, Sweden and the Netherlands.
metadata.scope: The pack separates public PAYG, notional-account, occupational funded and voluntary arrangements. It includes only indicators with an explicit definition and observed year.

comparabilityScale.high: The source uses one definition and one observation year for all four countries.
comparabilityScale.medium: The source is harmonised, but country rules, model assumptions or scheme mix limit interpretation.
comparabilityScale.low: The concepts or observation years differ materially. Use the values as context, not as a league table.

metadata.sourcePolicy: Primary statistical and institutional sources are preferred: OECD, Eurostat, Swiss Federal Social Insurance Office, Swedish Pensions Agency and government, Dutch central bank and Social Insurance Bank, and COVIP.
metadata.importantCaveat: OECD replacement rates and model retirement ages are projections for a stylised full-career worker. They are not observed outcomes for current retirees.

IT.name: Italy
IT.systemSummary: The public first pillar is a PAYG system with a long transition from legacy defined-benefit rules to the notional defined-contribution (NDC) method introduced in 1995. Supplementary occupational funds and personal products are funded and generally voluntary, with private-sector TFR severance pay able to flow into a supplementary fund.

retirementRules.note: The ordinary statutory age and the OECD model age are different concepts. The country note also describes an early route from age 64 subject to contribution conditions.

first.label: Public first pillar
first.funding: PAYG with legacy defined-benefit rules and an NDC transition
first.details: INPS public pensions. The NDC transition is not yet complete; OECD expects full NDC calculation for new pensioners around 2040.

second.label: Supplementary occupational pensions
second.funding: funded collective or individual pension funds
second.details: Private-sector TFR can be transferred to a supplementary fund by explicit choice or silent-assent rules. COVIP supervises supplementary schemes.

third.label: Voluntary personal savings
third.details: Personal pension products and other savings outside mandatory public insurance.

mechanisms: NDC notional-account calculation
Annuity conversion and life-expectancy adjustments
Retirement-age link to life expectancy
automaticStabilizers.policyCaveat: The OECD country note says the age link was suspended for 2019-2026 and describes a planned restoration in 2027. Treat that date as policy context, not as a guaranteed future outcome.

countryNotes: OECD reports public expenditure on cash old-age and survivor benefits at about 16% of GDP and says at least one quarter is not financed by pension contributions.

COVIP's current glossary describes automatic enrolment for private-sector employees first hired after 30 June 2026 unless they opt out or choose another fund within 60 days. The OECD coverage observation predates this change.

CH.name: Switzerland
CH.systemSummary: Switzerland has three pillars. The first pillar, OASI/AVS, is public and PAYG. The second pillar, occupational BVG/LPP, is a funded capitalisation system for employees above the entry threshold. The third pillar consists of voluntary funded individual savings, including pillars 3a and 3b.

retirementRules.note: AVS/AHV21 brings the reference age to 65 with a gradual transition for women. The OECD model table reflects the rules used for a person retiring in 2024, so it still reports a 64 normal age for women.

first.label: OASI/AVS public first pillar
first.details: Current contributions flow directly to current pensioners. OASI funds are not invested as individual retirement assets.

second.label: BVG/LPP occupational pension
second.mandate: mandatory above the statutory entry threshold
second.funding: funded capitalisation with individual savings capital and interest
second.details: The 2025 entry threshold is CHF 22,680 from one employer. The second pillar complements OASI/AVS.

third.label: Pillars 3a and 3b
third.details: Voluntary private provision outside the mandatory first and second pillars.

mechanisms: Reference-age reform and transitional rules
PAYG sensitivity to the contributor-to-pensioner ratio and economic growth
Funded second-pillar accumulation through contributions and interest
automaticStabilizers.note: The reviewed sources do not identify an automatic PAYG balance-index mechanism equivalent to Sweden's balance brake.

countryNotes: The Swiss first pillar is PAYG even though Switzerland has very high pension-provider assets relative to GDP. Do not treat the first pillar as a funded individual account.
The Federal Social Insurance Office says the federal government covers just over one-fifth of OASI expenses.

SE.name: Sweden
SE.systemSummary: Sweden combines a public NDC income pension financed on a PAYG basis, a funded public premium pension, a guarantee pension and broad occupational pensions. Personal savings are voluntary. The public contribution is split between 16% for the income pension and 2.5% for the premium pension.

retirementRules.note: Sweden has no fixed retirement age. The public pension can start from 63 under the rules described by the Pensions Agency, while age limits and the guarantee-pension age are linked to life expectancy from 2026.

first.label: Public income, premium and guarantee pensions
first.funding: PAYG NDC income pension plus funded premium pension and tax-financed guarantee pension
first.details: Each year 16% of pensionable income is allocated to the income pension and 2.5% to the premium pension, where the individual can choose funds or use AP7.

second.label: Occupational pension
second.details: Occupational pensions cover the vast majority of workers. Common contribution levels are about 4.5% to 6%, and the government brief reports occupational assets at about 75% of GDP at end-2024.

third.label: Personal savings
third.details: Private saving outside the public and occupational systems.

mechanisms: Automatic balancing of the income-pension system
Balance index that reduces indexation when liabilities exceed assets
Annuity divisors and age links based on life expectancy

countryNotes: The public premium pension and occupational schemes mean that Sweden is not a pure PAYG model. OECD reports public pension reserve funds separately from pension-provider assets.

The Swedish government brief reports public premium-pension assets at about 45% of GDP, public buffer funds at about 33% of GDP and public plus occupational assets at about 155% of GDP. These components overlap with, and are explained separately from, the OECD asset metric.

NL.name: Netherlands
NL.systemSummary: The Netherlands has a residence-linked AOW state pension financed on a PAYG basis, a very broad workplace pension pillar that is generally mandatory through sector or employer arrangements, and voluntary individual products. The workplace pillar is transitioning from collective defined-benefit promises to defined-contribution arrangements under the Future Pensions Act.

retirementRules.aowAgeCohortNote: AOW age is 67 for some 1957-1960 birth cohorts and 67 years and 3 months for January 1961 to September 1964 cohorts; later ages are linked to life expectancy.

first.label: AOW state pension
first.mandate: compulsory social insurance for insured residents and workers
first.details: Current workers' contributions finance current AOW pensions. Full entitlement depends on insured residence or work history.

second.label: Workplace pension
second.mandate: quasi-mandatory where a sector or employer arrangement applies
second.funding: funded occupational arrangements transitioning to defined contribution
second.details: The Future Pensions Act took effect on 1 July 2023. DNB says all funds must comply by 1 January 2028 at the latest, with no guarantee of a fixed pension amount under the new system.

third.label: Individual pension products
third.details: Individual income products and other private savings outside AOW and workplace pensions.

mechanisms: AOW age link to life expectancy
Funded workplace-pension return and risk-sharing rules under the new defined-contribution system
Transition compensation and fund-level implementation rules
automaticStabilizers.note: The reviewed sources do not identify a single automatic PAYG balance-index rule for AOW comparable to Sweden's balance brake.

countryNotes: The high Dutch pension-provider asset ratio largely reflects the funded workplace pillar. It should not be read as funded financing of AOW.
The 97.4% OECD coverage value is for a mandatory or quasi-mandatory occupational plan and uses 2023 data, while other countries in the table use 2024 or different plan categories.

comparableMetrics.label: Public expenditure on cash old-age and survivor benefits
comparableMetrics.definition: Public expenditure on cash old-age and survivor benefits, as defined in OECD Table 8.2.
notes: The OECD table reports the latest observation as 2021 for all four countries. It is not a measure of total pension spending in every national accounting definition.

comparableMetrics.label: Assets of pension providers
comparableMetrics.yearQualifier: End-2024 or latest available in the OECD table
comparableMetrics.definition: Assets of pension providers in asset-backed pension arrangements, including public or private occupational and personal arrangements. Public pension reserve funds that back unfunded or PAYG schemes are reported separately.
notes: These are not total household retirement wealth and do not mean that each country's public first pillar is funded.

comparableMetrics.label: Public pension reserve fund assets
comparableMetrics.yearQualifier: End-2024 or latest available in the OECD table
comparableMetrics.definition: Assets of public pension reserve funds supporting unfunded or PAYG public arrangements. These assets do not represent individual funded pension entitlements.

missingReasons.NL: Not applicable in the OECD table

notes: Keep this series separate from pension-provider assets. A null means not applicable or unavailable, not zero.

comparableMetrics.label: Effective mandatory pension contribution rate
comparableMetrics.definition: OECD effective total contribution rate for mandatory and quasi-mandatory pension schemes for private-sector workers, adjusted for earnings ceilings where applicable.
notes: Rates can include other social-insurance components or country-specific scheme features. Italy's rate also finances disability or invalidity benefits, and Swiss rates vary by age and earnings.

comparableMetrics.label: OECD model normal retirement age
comparableMetrics.definition: Eligibility age for all mandatory components without penalty for a person starting work at age 22 and retiring in 2024 after an uninterrupted full career. The OECD selects the maximum age when schemes differ.
notes: This is a harmonised model concept, not a single statutory age. It can differ from the legal age and from the age at which people actually claim or leave work.

comparableMetrics.label: Statutory or reference retirement age
comparableMetrics.definition: A national legal or reference age selected for context. Because Sweden has no fixed retirement age and the other systems use different legal concepts, values are not a harmonised ranking.

details.IT: Ordinary statutory age reported by OECD for 2025; early routes have contribution conditions.
details.CH: Reference age after AVS/AHV21, with transitional rules for women.
details.SE: No fixed statutory retirement age; public pension claim can start from 63 under the cited 2025 rules.
details.NL: AOW age is cohort-dependent: 67 for some cohorts and 67 years 3 months for later cohorts covered by the cited SVB table.

comparableMetrics.label: Effective age of labour-market exit
comparableMetrics.definition: OECD estimate of the average age of exit from the labour force for workers aged 40 and over, inferred from participation-rate changes. It is not a pension-claiming age.
notes: OECD advises caution with absolute levels; comparisons are more robust than country-specific estimates.

comparableMetrics.label: Gross pension replacement rate for an average earner
comparableMetrics.definition: OECD modelled gross pension entitlement relative to individual gross earnings for a full-career average earner in mandatory schemes at the current normal retirement age.
notes: This is a modelled entitlement, not an observed outcome. It does not make voluntary savings comparable across countries and cannot capture every household's tax or career history.

comparableMetrics.label: Net pension replacement rate for an average earner
comparableMetrics.definition: OECD modelled net pension entitlement relative to individual net earnings for a full-career average earner in mandatory schemes at the current normal retirement age, after taxes and social contributions.
notes: Tax treatment and mandatory-scheme composition are built into the OECD model. Treat values as scenario outputs rather than promises to an actual retiree.

comparableMetrics.label: Old-age dependency ratio
comparableMetrics.definition: Eurostat indicator OLDDEP1: population aged 65 years or over divided by population aged 15 to 64 years.
notes: This is a demographic pressure indicator, not a pension-system dependency ratio and not a forecast of contribution adequacy.

comparableMetrics.label: Pension-plan coverage among people aged 15 to 64
comparableMetrics.definition: OECD share of the population aged 15 to 64 with assets or accrued rights in a pension plan. Plan categories can overlap and are not a universal active-contributor rate.

IT.note: OECD reports mandatory or quasi-mandatory occupational coverage as not applicable; the voluntary categories can overlap.

notes: The OECD table uses 2023 for Dutch and Swiss occupational observations and 2024 for Italian and Swedish observations. Sweden's value is public PPS coverage, not occupational coverage. Do not add categories or compare them as if they measured the same pillar.

keyContrasts.title: Switzerland pairs a PAYG first pillar with a large funded second pillar
keyContrasts.evidence: BSV states that OASI/AVS contributions flow directly to current pensioners and are not invested, while occupational BVG/LPP savings are funded. OECD pension-provider assets are 166.9% of GDP, so this high asset ratio must not be interpreted as funded financing of OASI.

keyContrasts.title: Italy has the highest public cash pension expenditure in this group
keyContrasts.evidence: OECD reports 16.1% of GDP in 2021 for Italy, compared with 8.0% in Sweden, 6.6% in Switzerland and 6.4% in the Netherlands. Italy also has the highest effective mandatory contribution rate at 33.0% of gross average earnings in the OECD table.

keyContrasts.title: Funded asset depth is much greater in Switzerland, the Netherlands and Sweden than in Italy
keyContrasts.evidence: OECD pension-provider assets are 166.9% of GDP in Switzerland, 150.9% in the Netherlands, 115.8% in Sweden and 11.7% in Italy. These figures describe funded providers, not the value of PAYG promises.

keyContrasts.title: Sweden splits the public contribution between PAYG NDC and funded premium pension
keyContrasts.evidence: The Swedish Pensions Agency and government brief describe an 18.5% public contribution: 16% to the PAYG income pension and 2.5% to the funded premium pension. Automatic balancing adjusts the income-pension index when liabilities exceed assets.

keyContrasts.title: The Dutch funded workplace pillar is moving to defined contribution
keyContrasts.evidence: DNB says the Future Pensions Act took effect on 1 July 2023 and that pension funds must comply by 1 January 2028 at the latest. The new arrangements do not guarantee a fixed pension amount, while AOW remains a separate PAYG state pension.

keyContrasts.title: Italy faces the highest demographic old-age dependency ratio
keyContrasts.evidence: Eurostat's 2025 OLDDEP1 ratio is 39.0% in Italy, versus 33.4% in Sweden, 32.4% in the Netherlands and 29.8% in Switzerland.

keyContrasts.title: A PAYG-to-funded shift creates a transition financing cost
keyContrasts.evidence: OECD and World Bank guidance explains that diverting current contributions into funded accounts creates a financing gap while legacy PAYG claims remain payable. Workers or taxpayers can face a double burden, financing both the residual PAYG system and new funded saving. The pack does not assign a numeric transition cost to any country because no harmonised country estimate was found in the reviewed sources.

methodologyNotes: Country order is fixed as Italy, Switzerland, Sweden and the Netherlands. ISO2 codes are used in every comparable metric.
A high comparability label means the source definition and observation year align. Medium and low labels are intentional warnings, not missing data.

Public expenditure is OECD cash old-age and survivor benefits for 2021. Pension-provider assets are funded provider assets for end-2024 or latest and are kept separate from public pension reserve funds.
A public pension reserve fund is not an individual funded account. Switzerland's OASI first pillar remains PAYG despite the country's high funded provider assets.
Contribution rates are OECD effective totals for mandatory and quasi-mandatory schemes. National rates can include disability, invalidity or other social insurance, and ceilings and age bands differ.
OECD replacement rates and model retirement ages use a stylised full-career average earner. They are not observed replacement rates, legal ages in every country or individual forecasts.
Statutory or reference ages are deliberately separate from effective labour-market exit ages. Sweden has no fixed retirement age, and Dutch AOW age is cohort-dependent.

Coverage observations are plan-member or accrued-right measures among people aged 15 to 64. Plan categories can overlap, and OECD observation years differ for Italy, Switzerland, Sweden and the Netherlands.

The transition-cost contrast is directional. OECD and World Bank sources explain the financing mechanism, but this pack does not invent a country-specific euro estimate without a harmonised primary estimate.
Null values mean not applicable, unavailable or not aligned in the cited source. They must not be rendered as zero.
All URLs were collected from the cited institutional pages or APIs and reviewed on 2026-08-23.
